chapter_theme: The first half of the hunters' song: at Aiyai's shrine in the dry country, where Kovalan and Kannaki rest, the possessed Saalini demands the goddess's due because the hunters' raids have failed; they dress a maiden of their clan as Kotravai and worship her; Saalini, still possessed, hails Kannaki as the jewel of the world, which Kannaki takes for confusion; and the hunters sing the goddess as Shiva's half, Mal's sister, the slayer of the buffalo-demon and the light above the Vedas, and their own clan as the first of clans through the girl who wears her form.

cast.role: Kovalan's wife, walking with him to Madurai
son of the merchant Maasaathuvan, Kannaki's husband
the ascetic woman travelling with Kovalan and Kannaki to Madurai
a woman of the hunters' fighting clan, bound to its old duty to the goddess, who is possessed in the rite
the bow-bearing hunters of the dry country, who sing the vari
the hunter women who carry the offerings
the maiden of the hunters' clan dressed as the goddess
the war goddess of the dry country, also called Aiyai, the goddess of the stag

silappathikaram:12:1-19.reading: Footsore from the road under the scorching sun, Kannaki rests with her husband in a corner of Aiyai's shrine, while Saalini, a woman of the hunters' fighting clan bound to its old duty to the goddess, is seized by the deity, dances in the village common and says that the goddess of the stag gives victory to the bow only when her due is paid, since the hunters' cattle-raids have failed and they have fallen quiet.
silappathikaram:12:1-19.nuance: Lines 12-15 set the cause of the rite: the herds in the big villages thrive, the hunters' common lies waste, and the fighting clan, its raiding yielding nothing, has subsided 'like a clan of dharma' (அறக்குடி போல, line 15), so the poet makes peace the hunters' misfortune. Lines 16-19 are Saalini's words, closed by எனவாங்கு; the sense of 18-19 (மட்டுண் வாழ்க்கை, கட்டுண் மாக்கள் கடந்தரும்) is not secure, but the demand is plain: the goddess's debt (கடன்) must be paid before she gives victory.
silappathikaram:12:1-19.event: Kovalan and Kannaki rest at Aiyai's shrine, and Saalini, possessed by the goddess, dances in the hunters' common and says the goddess will give victory only when her due is paid.

claims.claim: the goddess of the stag grants victory in war only to those who pay her due offering

silappathikaram:12:1-19.unit_note: Boundary moved from 15 to 19: line 15 closes the narrator's sentence, but Saalini's speech runs 16-19 and is closed by எனவாங்கு (line 19); the new dressing sentence begins at line 20.

silappathikaram:12:20-44.reading: The hunters take a maiden of their old unyielding clan, bind her hair with a young white snake, set a boar's curved tusk on it like the crescent moon, hang a row of tiger's teeth on her as a tali, gird her with a striped and spotted skin, put a bow in her hand and seat her on a stag with twisted horns, and, with dolls, parrots, jungle fowl, peacocks, balls and play-stones laid before her and the women of the clan carrying colours, powders, sandal, boiled grain, sesame cakes, rich rice, flowers and incense behind, they sound drums, horns, flutes and bells and worship the goddess of the stag at her altar of bought offerings.
silappathikaram:12:20-44.nuance: The unit turns a hunter girl into the goddess by costume: each item (snake, boar tusk as crescent, tiger teeth, skin girdle, bow, stag mount) is one of the goddess's emblems that the later songs give back to the goddess herself (lines 58-62, 99-104). The opening phrase (இட்டுத் தலையெண்ணும் எயினரல்லது சுட்டுத் தலைபோகா, lines 20-21) praises the girl's clan as one that never bows its head to any but its own, but the exact sense of the two head-phrases is not secure. விலைப்பலி (line 43) is an offering given in return, as a price, which fits Saalini's talk of the goddess's due.
silappathikaram:12:20-44.event: The hunters dress a maiden of their clan as the goddess, seat her on a stag, and with offerings, drums and horns worship the goddess at her altar.
silappathikaram:12:20-44.unit_note: Boundary moved from 34 to 44 (and 16 to 20): the old break at 34 fell in the middle of the list of gifts (break score 0 at 35), while line 44 closes the worship of the goddess (கைதொழு தேத்தி) before the scene turns to Kannaki at line 45.

silappathikaram:12:45-53.reading: As Kannaki, her small feet aching, sits with her husband, the possessed Saalini points to her and says that this woman is the goddess of Kongu and of the western hills, the shoot of the penance done by the Tamil maiden, a single great jewel risen to light the world; Kannaki, thinking the old wise woman has spoken in confusion, shrinks behind her husband's broad back with the shy smile of a stranger.
silappathikaram:12:45-53.nuance: This is the first time in the story anyone calls Kannaki divine, and it comes from a possessed hunter woman in a desert shrine, not from the great. Kannaki's own judgement is that the words are பேதுறவு, bewilderment (line 51); the story will prove the priestess right. The three regions she names (கொங்கு, குடமலை, தென்றமிழ், lines 47-48) are where Kannaki will later be worshipped, so the speech reads as prophecy, though the unit itself does not say so.
silappathikaram:12:45-53.event: Possessed, Saalini hails Kannaki as a great jewel born for the world, and Kannaki, taking the words for confusion, hides behind her husband and smiles.
silappathikaram:12:45-53.unit_note: Boundary moved from 50 to 53 (and 45 begins the unit): Saalini's speech runs 47-50 and is closed by the narrator at 51 (என்று); lines 52-53 give Kannaki's response, ending with the clause அரும்பினள் நிற்ப, after which the list of the goddess's epithets begins at 54.

silappathikaram:12:54-74.reading: The goddess is hailed in a long chain of names: she wears the crescent, has the unwinking eye in her split forehead, coral lips and white teeth, a throat dark from the poison, bends the great mountain with a snake for string, wears a cobra as breast band, holds the trident, wears the elephant's hide and the lion's skin, is Kotravai of the true sword, the maiden standing on the head of the two-formed asura, Amari, Kumari, Gauri, Samari, Shooli, Neeli, the younger kin of Mal, Aiyai, the red one, the doll of the leaping stag; and it is declared that she, in the maiden's guise come for her people to worship, has given her grace and the vari rite has borne fruit.
silappathikaram:12:54-74.nuance: The epithets fuse the hunters' war goddess with Shiva (crescent, forehead eye, dark throat, bending Meru with a snake, elephant hide), with the slayer of the buffalo-demon (line 65-66) and with Vishnu, whose younger kin she is called (மாலவற் கிளங்கிளை, line 68). The unit ends with எனவே, so these are someone's words, most likely the hunters' or Saalini's; the text does not name the speaker.
silappathikaram:12:54-74.event: The goddess in the guise of a maiden is declared to have given her grace, and the vari rite is said to have succeeded.
silappathikaram:12:54-74.unit_note: Unit begins at 54 instead of 51: lines 51-53 close Saalini's speech and give Kannaki's response (now in 45-53); the chain of the goddess's names starts at line 54 and runs to the closing எனவே at 74.

silappathikaram:12:75-78.reading: The first song of the court: before the shrine of the goddess who rules half the body of the forehead-eyed god, nagam and narantham spread their scent, aa and sandal trees grow tall everywhere, and red deer and other beasts crowd together.

silappathikaram:12:79-82.reading: The second song: before the shrine of the goddess whose matted hair holds the moon, the vengai sheds its golden flowers, the red-petalled silk-cotton heaps its blossoms and the punku scatters white puffed-rice flowers.

silappathikaram:12:83-86.reading: The third song: before the shrine of the goddess who is the kin of Tirumal, maravam, paathiri, punnai, kuravam and kongam bloom on their branches and swarms of bees hum together like a yazh.
silappathikaram:12:83-86.nuance: The three refrains give the goddess's court to three figures in turn: Shiva's half (line 78), the one with the moon in her matted hair (line 82), and the kin of Mal (line 86), so the court of the forest goddess is placed between the two great gods.

silappathikaram:12:87-90.reading: The singers ask what penance this golden-bangled girl did, that she stands wearing Kotravai's own adornment, and answer that the clan of bowmen hunters in which she was born is the clan among clans.
silappathikaram:12:87-90.nuance: The question (தவமென்னை கொல்லோ) treats the girl's present glory as the fruit of some penance, and the answer moves the credit from her to her birth-clan: the girl's merit makes the hunters' clan the first of clans. The same pattern is sung twice more with different names for goddess and clan (91-94, 95-98).

claims.claim: a clan becomes the first of clans through a daughter born in it who bears the goddess's form

silappathikaram:12:91-94.reading: The second stanza asks what penance this girl did, that she stands wearing the adornment of Aiyai, and answers that the clan of the Eyinar of the shooting bow, in which she was born, is the clan among clans.

silappathikaram:12:95-98.reading: The third stanza asks what penance this well-bangled girl did, that she stands wearing the adornment of the doll of the leaping stag, and answers that the clan of the Eyinar with bamboo bows, in which she was born, is the clan among clans.

silappathikaram:12:99-102.reading: The singers tell the goddess that she stands on the black head of the forest buffalo, wrapped in an elephant's hide and girt with a tiger's skin, and that, worshipped by the gods, she stands unshaken as the secret beyond the Vedas and the shoot of wisdom.
silappathikaram:12:99-102.nuance: The same stanza joins the cult image (the buffalo's head under her feet, the hides) to the highest doctrinal title: மறைமேல் மறை, the mystery above the Veda. Elephant hide and tiger skin are Shiva's emblems elsewhere, here worn by the goddess.

claims.claim: the goddess is the hidden truth above the Vedas and the shoot of wisdom

silappathikaram:12:103-106.reading: The singers tell the goddess that, sword in her bangled hand, she killed the great buffalo-demon and stands on the black stag with twisted horns, and that she abides as the light of spreading rays in the heart-lotus of Hari, Hara and the one on the flower.
silappathikaram:12:103-106.nuance: The claim places the goddess as the light within all three gods, Vishnu, Shiva and Brahma alike, so she is not ranked under Shiva here; the saiva tag on the claim follows the cycle's other stanzas (99, 109), which make her Shiva's, and should be read with that caution.

claims.claim: the goddess abides as the light in the hearts of Hari, Hara and Brahma

silappathikaram:12:107-110.reading: The singers tell the goddess that, holding conch, discus and lotus in her hands, she stands on the angry bull of the red-eyed one, and that she stands as the woman's form in the share of the forehead-eyed god who wears the Ganga in his hair, praised by the Veda.
silappathikaram:12:107-110.nuance: The goddess carries Vishnu's conch and discus while standing as the left half of Shiva, so one stanza gives her both great gods. The phrase செங்கண் அரிமால் சினவிடை (line 108) can be read as the angry bull or as a lion with Mal's name; the mount is not certain.

claims.claim: the goddess is the woman's form in the half of Shiva's body, praised by the Veda

silappathikaram:12:111-115.reading: Thus, with a thick garland of kondrai and tulasi flowers woven together laid on her shoulders, the maiden enters the dance that the goddess in maiden form danced for the gods when the asuras withered.
silappathikaram:12:111-115.nuance: The garland joins Shiva's kondrai and Vishnu's tulasi, as the songs before it joined the two gods' emblems. Whether the subject of கூத்துள் படுமே is the dressed hunter girl entering the dance, or the song itself counting as part of the goddess's dance, is not clear from the lines.
silappathikaram:12:111-115.event: Garlanded with kondrai and tulasi, the dressed maiden enters the goddess's victory dance.

links.note: Saalini, possessed, calls Kannaki a goddess and the jewel of the world, and Kannaki hides behind her husband; at the Pandya's gate the gatekeeper can describe Kannaki only by saying she is not Kotravai on the bleeding pedestal, nor Kali who tore Daruka's chest.
links.teaches: The divinity a hunter priestess proclaims in a desert shrine, and which Kannaki herself laughs off as confusion, becomes visible to a stranger at the palace door, so the pair shows the story turning Saalini's words into what others see, and the shy wife into a figure that can only be named by the war goddess she is denied to be.

links.note: The patikam opens with the hill kuravar telling Ilango of the one-breasted pathini taken to heaven before their eyes; the vari has desert hunters' priestess first naming Kannaki divine.
links.teaches: Both the frame and the first sign within the story put Kannaki's divinity in the mouths of forest and hill folk, before any king or sage acknowledges it, so the pairing shows the epic consistently letting the people of the wilds be the first witnesses of the pathini.

links.note: The Ainkurunuru friend asks whether it is a kindness if the old velan of an unerring tradition casts his beads and says the girl's sickness is Murugu; the epic's old wise woman of the clan's ancient duty, possessed, declares Kannaki divine and Kannaki calls it confusion.
links.teaches: In the akam convention the possessed diviner of an old line is the one who gets it wrong, mistaking love for a god's seizure, while in the epic the possessed old woman's word is the true one and the hearer's doubt is the mistake, so the pairing shows the epic reversing the Sangam irony about divination to make it carry prophecy.

gains.a: Kannaki's dismissal of the speech as பேதுறவு reads as a known stance, the akam scepticism toward the diviner, which the story will overturn
gains.b: the friend's mockery of the unerring velan gains a later counter-case where the same kind of possessed elder speaks truly

links.note: The Murukatruppadai hails Murugan among his titles as son of the banyan god, son of the mountain's daughter, and child of Kotravai of victorious war; the vari heaps on Kotravai herself the names of Gauri, Shiva's emblems and the title of Mal's younger kin.
links.teaches: The Sangam guide poem joins Kotravai to the Saiva household through her son, listing her beside the mountain daughter as Murugan's mother, while the epic's hunters make Kotravai herself absorb Gauri, Shiva's emblems and Vishnu's kinship, so the pair shows the war goddess of the wilds drawn into the great gods' family by two different routes.

gains.a: the epic's fusion of names appears as the later step of a joining already begun in the Sangam praise of Murugan as Kotravai's son
gains.b: the bare title கொற்றவை சிறுவ gains the full portrait of the mother it names, with her mount, weapons and the cult that worships her

links.note: Tirumular lists the goddess's names (Tripurai, Sundari, Narani, Manonmani and others) and says by them the great one stands as many; the vari lists Amari, Kumari, Gauri, Samari, Shooli, Neeli and others for the hunters' goddess of the stag.
links.teaches: Both pile names on one goddess, but the hunters' names come from her weapons, mounts, hides and battle with the asura and end in a rite where a girl wears them, while Tirumular's end in the doctrine that one power stands as many, so the pair shows the same device of the name-chain serving a public rite of costume and possession in one text and an inner theology of a single Shakti in the other.

gains.a: the vari's chain of names is seen to make no doctrinal claim of oneness; it names a goddess to be worn and worshipped
gains.b: Tirumular's doctrine that the one stands as many gains an older, folk chain of names (குமரி, கவுரி, நீலி) that it gathers into his single Shakti

links.note: Tirumular makes knowledge of the First, the meaning of the Veda, together with Parashakti abiding in his half, the mark of the one in niyama; the vari makes the hunters' war goddess the woman's form in the half of the forehead-eyed god, praised by the Veda, while carrying Vishnu's conch and discus.
links.teaches: The half-woman form that Tirumular holds as an object of contemplative knowledge is, in the hunters' song, a goddess with Vishnu's weapons on a fighting mount, so the pair shows the same Saiva image serving yogic discipline in one text and a war cult that will not keep her to one god in the other.

gains.a: the stanza's line on Shiva's half is shown to be the Saiva doctrinal image, and its addition of Vishnu's weapons stands out against it
gains.b: the verse's பாதியுள் மன்னும் பரசக்தி gains an early witness outside the Saiva canon, worshipped by hunters with offerings rather than known in niyama

links.note: The couplet says birth is alike for all beings and distinction comes from the difference in deeds; the vari credits a girl's penance with her glory and then declares her birth-clan, the bow-wielding hunters, the clan among clans.
links.teaches: The song agrees that distinction comes from a deed, the girl's penance, but hands that distinction straight back to the birth-group, the move the couplet's rule forbids, so the pair shows how a low-ranked clan claims rank through one daughter's merit rather than by denying that birth confers it.

gains.a: the hunters' boast is shown to rest on a deed and not on birth alone, and to turn that deed into a clan's rank
gains.b: the couplet's rule gains a case that tests it, where an individual deed's distinction is claimed for a whole clan of a lowly calling

new_concepts.gloss: the war goddess of the dry country, worshipped by the hunters with offerings for victory, also called Aiyai and the goddess of the stag
new_concepts.label_source: the unit's own word (கொற்றவை, lines 64 and 87; ஐயை, lines 4, 69 and 91)

new_concepts.gloss: dance-drama as a learned art, with its kinds, rules, gestures and accompanying music, performed before the king
new_concepts.label_source: the unit's own word (கூத்துள், line 115); id and gloss as declared in Silappathikaram chapter 4

source_issues: The show header gives the kaathai 168 lines but says the edition's printed last line number is 70, so the edition's printed line numbers do not match the core's count; line numbers here are the core's.
The four akaval units were cut at weak breaks (break score 0 at line 35, and 16 and 51 fall inside speeches); they were moved to 1-19, 20-44, 45-53 and 54-74.
Lines 75-86 carry the rubric உரைப்பாட்டுமடை together with வேறு, though they are three regular sung stanzas; the rubric may belong to a prose passage not in the core.
